name: Basic Computer Skills
objectives: Given a desktop or laptop computer, name its main parts, turn it on and sign in, without help, naming the screen, keyboard, mouse or trackpad and the power button
Using a mouse or trackpad, point, click, double-click, right-click and scroll, doing each action correctly when asked
Using the keyboard, type a sentence with capital letters, spaces and punctuation and fix mistakes, with a capital at the start of each sentence and every mistake fixed with Backspace or undo
On a Windows or Mac computer, open an app by name, resize or minimize its window, bring it back and close it, without help
Given a short note to save, create a folder, save the note in it with a clear name and find it again, with the file in the right folder and opened again later
When a computer needs care or has a problem, install updates, restart, shut down properly and choose a safe place to get help, using the menu to shut down and never calling a number from a pop-up

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The parts of a computer, and turning it on
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the main parts of a computer, turn it on and sign in.
This lesson builds toward: Given a desktop or laptop computer, you will name its main parts, turn it on and sign in, without help, naming the screen, keyboard, mouse or trackpad and the power button.
A desktop computer has a screen (monitor), a keyboard, a mouse and a box or screen that holds the computer itself. A laptop has all of these in one piece that folds open; instead of a mouse it has a flat touch pad called a trackpad.
To turn it on, press the power button once. It usually has a circle with a line through the top. On a laptop it is often at the top right of the keyboard or on the side. Wait for the screen to wake up.
Most computers then ask you to sign in with a password or PIN. Type it and press Enter. On a shared computer, like one at a library, the staff will tell you how to sign in.
Step by step:
- Find the power button (a circle with a line at the top).
- Press it once and let go.
- Wait for the sign-in screen.
- Type your password or PIN and press Enter.
Words to know:
- Monitor: the screen of a desktop computer.
- Laptop: a computer that folds open, with the screen and keyboard in one piece.
- Trackpad: the flat touch pad on a laptop that works like a mouse.
- Sign in: type your password or PIN so the computer knows it is you.
Try it now: Point to the screen, keyboard and mouse (or trackpad) on a computer near you. Find the power button, turn the computer on and sign in.
You can now name the parts of a computer, turn it on and sign in.

check.why: The monitor is the screen where you see your work.

check.q: You want to use a computer at the library and it asks for a sign-in. What would you do?
options: Hold the power button until it turns off
Type random letters until it opens
Ask the staff how to sign in
check.why: On a shared computer, the staff will tell you how to sign in.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Using the mouse or trackpad
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Point, click, double-click, right-click and scroll.
This lesson builds toward: Using a mouse or trackpad, you will point, click, double-click, right-click and scroll, doing each action correctly when asked.
The mouse moves the pointer, the small arrow on the screen. Rest your hand on the mouse and slide it gently on the table; the arrow follows. If you run out of room, lift the mouse and put it back down in the middle.
Click: press the left button once to choose something. Double-click: press the left button twice quickly to open something, like a folder. Right-click: press the right button once to see a short menu of choices. Scroll: roll the small wheel between the buttons to move a page up or down.
On a laptop trackpad, slide one finger to move the arrow, tap or press once to click, and slide two fingers up or down to scroll. To right-click, tap with two fingers.
Step by step:
- Slide the mouse to move the arrow.
- Click: press the left button once.
- Double-click: press the left button twice quickly.
- Right-click: press the right button once for a menu.
- Scroll: roll the wheel, or slide two fingers on a trackpad.
Words to know:
- Pointer: the small arrow on the screen that moves with the mouse.
- Click: press the left mouse button once.
- Double-click: press the left button twice quickly to open something.
- Right-click: press the right button to see a menu of choices.
- Scroll: move a page up or down.
Try it now: Open any web page or document. Scroll down and back up. Right-click on an empty spot and read the menu, then press the Esc key to close it. Double-click a word to select it.
You can now point, click, double-click, right-click and scroll with a mouse or trackpad.

options: Moves a page up or down
check.why: Rolling the mouse wheel, or sliding two fingers on a trackpad, moves the page.

check.q: On a laptop trackpad, you want to see the short menu of choices. What would you do?
check.why: On a trackpad, a two-finger tap is a right-click.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Typing with the keyboard
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Type a sentence with capital letters, spaces and punctuation, and fix mistakes.
This lesson builds toward: Using the keyboard, you will type a sentence with capital letters, spaces and punctuation and fix mistakes, with a capital at the start of each sentence and every mistake fixed with Backspace or undo.
The keyboard has letters, numbers and special keys. The long bar at the bottom is the Space bar. Enter (Return on a Mac) starts a new line or says "go". Backspace (Delete on a Mac) removes the letter to the left of the blinking line, called the cursor.
For one capital letter, hold Shift and press the letter. Caps Lock makes every letter a capital until you press it again. Shift also types the top symbol on a key, like ? or !.
Shortcuts save time. On Windows use Ctrl; on a Mac use Command. Ctrl+Z undoes a mistake, Ctrl+C copies, Ctrl+V pastes and Ctrl+S saves.
Step by step:
- Click where you want to type; the cursor blinks there.
- Hold Shift and press a letter for a capital.
- Press the Space bar between words.
- Press Backspace (Delete on Mac) to fix a mistake.
- Press Enter (Return on Mac) for a new line.
Words to know:
- Cursor: the blinking line that shows where your typing will go.
- Shift: the key you hold for a capital letter or a top symbol.
- Backspace: the key that deletes the letter to the left (Delete on a Mac).
- Shortcut: a key combination that does a job quickly, like Ctrl+S to save.
Try it now: Open a search box or a blank document and type: My name is ___ and I am learning computers! Use a capital letter at the start, then delete one word with Backspace and type it again.
You can now type sentences with capitals and punctuation, fix mistakes and use common shortcuts.

check.q: What does Ctrl+C do on Windows?
Everything you type is coming out in capital letters. What would you do?
options: Press Caps Lock again to turn it off
check.why: Caps Lock makes every letter a capital until you press it again.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Opening apps and handling windows
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open an app, resize its window and close it.
This lesson builds toward: On a Windows or Mac computer, you will open an app by name, resize or minimize its window, bring it back and close it, without help.
Apps (programs) do jobs: a web browser for the internet, a writing app for notes, a photo app for pictures. On Windows, click the Start button (the Windows logo at the bottom of the screen) and type the app's name. On a Mac, click the magnifying glass at the top right (Spotlight), type the name and press Return.
Each app opens in a window. At the top corner are small buttons. On Windows, at the top right: a dash (minimize, hide it for now), a square (maximize, fill the screen) and an X (close). On a Mac, at the top left: red (close), yellow (minimize) and green (full screen).
Minimized apps wait on the taskbar (Windows, at the bottom) or the Dock (Mac). Click the app's icon there to bring it back.
Step by step:
- Windows: click Start and type the app name. Mac: click the magnifying glass and type the name.
- Press Enter or Return to open it.
- Use the minimize button to hide it.
- Click its icon on the taskbar or Dock to bring it back.
- Close it with X (Windows) or the red button (Mac).
Words to know:
- App / program: software that does a job, like writing or browsing.
- Window: the box an app opens in.
- Minimize: hide a window for now without closing it.
- Taskbar / Dock: the row of app icons at the bottom of the screen (Windows taskbar, Mac Dock).
Try it now: Open Notepad (Windows) or TextEdit (Mac) by typing its name in Start or Spotlight. Minimize it, bring it back from the taskbar or Dock, then make it fill the screen.
You can now open any app by name, move between windows and close them.

check.q: On Windows, what does the square button at the top right of a window do?
options: Makes the window fill the screen
check.why: The square is maximize; the dash hides the window and the X closes it.

check.q: You minimized your writing app and now want it back. What would you do?
options: Click its icon on the taskbar (Windows) or the Dock (Mac)
check.why: Minimized apps wait on the taskbar or Dock until you click them.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Saving and finding files in folders
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Save a note in a folder you made and find it again.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short note to save, you will create a folder, save the note in it with a clear name and find it again, with the file in the right folder and opened again later.
A file is one saved thing: a letter, a photo, a list. A folder holds files, like a drawer in a filing cabinet. The Documents folder is a good home for your files.
To make a folder: on Windows open File Explorer (the yellow folder icon), click Documents, then choose New and Folder. On a Mac open Finder (the blue face icon), click Documents, then open the File menu and choose New Folder. Type a name and press Enter or Return.
To save: press Ctrl+S (Command+S on a Mac). A box opens; choose the folder, type a clear file name like "Questions for Dr Lee", and click Save. To find a file later, open File Explorer or Finder and look in the folder, or type part of the name in the search box.
Step by step:
- Open File Explorer (Windows) or Finder (Mac).
- Go to Documents and make a new folder.
- In your app, press Ctrl+S (Command+S on Mac).
- Pick the folder, type a clear name, click Save.
- To find it: open the folder, or search for part of the name.
Words to know:
- File: one saved item, like a letter or photo.
- Folder: a place that holds files, like a drawer.
- File Explorer / Finder: the app for looking at files and folders (Windows / Mac).
Try it now: Make a folder called "Practice" in Documents. Type a short list in Notepad or TextEdit, save it in Practice as "My First Note", close the app, then find and open the file again.
You can now make folders, save files with clear names and find them again.

options: One saved thing, such as a letter, photo or list
The app that opens the internet
check.why: A file is one saved thing; a folder holds files.

check.q: You finished a note and want to keep it. What would you do?
options: Press Ctrl+S (Command+S on Mac), choose the folder, type a clear name and click Save
check.why: Saving puts the note in a folder with a name so you can find it later.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping your computer healthy
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Install updates, restart and shut down properly, and know where to get help.
This lesson builds toward: When a computer needs care or has a problem, you will install updates, restart, shut down properly and choose a safe place to get help, using the menu to shut down and never calling a number from a pop-up.
Updates fix problems and close security holes. On Windows, open Settings and choose Windows Update. On a Mac, open System Settings and choose General, then Software Update. Install updates when asked and let the computer restart.
If the computer is slow or something freezes, save your work and restart it. That fixes many problems. To shut down on Windows: Start, then the power icon, then Shut down. On a Mac: the Apple menu at the top left, then Shut Down. Do not just unplug it or hold the power button unless it is completely stuck.
If a pop-up says your computer has a virus and gives a phone number, do not call; close it. Ask for help from someone you trust, a library's tech help session, or the store where you bought the computer.
Step by step:
- Check for updates: Windows Update (Windows) or Software Update (Mac).
- Install them and let the computer restart.
- Slow or frozen? Save and restart.
- Shut down: Start, power icon, Shut down (Windows) or Apple menu, Shut Down (Mac).
- Need help? A trusted person, library tech help or the store.
Words to know:
- Update: a free fix from the maker that improves safety and features.
- Restart: turn the computer off and on again in one step.
- Shut down: turn the computer fully off the right way.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to spot, avoid and report tech support scams
Try it now: Final task: turn on and sign in, make a Practice folder, type and save a short note with capitals in Notepad or TextEdit, close it, find and open it again, check for updates, then shut down properly.
You can now use a computer from start to finish: sign in, work, save, find your files and shut down safely.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Turning on and signing in Needs help to turn on the computer or sign in. Turns on the computer and signs in without help. Also names the main parts of the computer. Folder and saved note The Practice folder or the saved note is missing, or the note has a name like Untitled. A Practice folder in Documents holds the note, saved with a clear name. Finds the file again using the search box as well as the folder. Typing the note The note is missing, or sentences have no capital letters. A short note with a capital at the start of each sentence and mistakes fixed. Also uses punctuation such as ? or ! correctly and uses Ctrl+Z (Command+Z) to undo. Opening and closing the app Cannot open Notepad or TextEdit, or cannot close it. Opens the app by name, closes it, then finds and opens the saved file. Also minimizes the window and brings it back from the taskbar or Dock. Shutting down The computer is unplugged or the power button is held down. Shuts down properly from the Start menu or Apple menu. Also checks for updates before shutting down. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where do you find updates on a Windows computer?
check.why: Windows updates are in Settings, under Windows Update.

check.q: You are done for the day on a Windows computer. What would you do?
options: Click Start, then the power icon, then Shut down
Close the lid while an app is saving
check.why: Shutting down from the menu is the proper way; unplugging can cause problems.
